newsitem.title: UK: UK pooled charity funds not investing ethically.
newsitem.headline: UK pooled charity funds not investing ethically.

text.p: Most UK pooled Charity Investment Funds (CIFs) are exposed to areas of corporate activity likely to conflict with their ethical objectives, according to a survey conducted by EIRIS, the Ethical Investment Research Service.

In a report released this week EIRIS said it examined the holdings of nine CIFs and Charifund, which although not strictly a CIF, was acknowledged by the UK Charity Commission as having comparable attributes.

CIFs, with assets of around 2.0 billion stg, are pooled investment funds similar to unit trusts, set up specially for charities. They were introduced to offer charities access to professional managers via a cost-effective structure which most could not offer or sustain on their own.

The EIRIS survey examines the extent to which CIFs invest in companies involved in seven areas: tobacco or alcohol production; intensive farming or animal testing; activities that may harm the environment; gambling; activities in countries with serious human rights problems, the military, and potential Third World exploitation.
"The survey shows that most of the CIFs have investments in all seven problem areas," said EIRIS. The Alpha Charity Fund had zero exposure to just one of the seven areas -- Animal Issues.

"Many of the charities that invest in CIFs are putting money into activities that arguably undermine their objectives," the report said. But it added that this left "a clear gap in the market for CIFs managed with ethical objectives in mind."
It did not examine whether the CIFs are investing with a "positive" ethical bias -- backing companies that avoid the problem areas it defined.

But the report identified rapid growth in the UK ethical investment sector since it was established in 1984. Over 1.0 billion stg is now invested in 27 ethical unit trusts and other funds, apart from CIFs, church and local authority money.
"The sector is predicted to grow faster in the future as it becomes more common for financial advisors and investment managers to ask clients about ethical concerns," EIRIS said.
CIFs are "special range investments", which are themselves constituted as charities. Their key advantages over general unit trusts are their lower fees and tax benefits.

But they are also restricted to putting at most 75 percent into "wider range" or more risky vehicles like unit trusts. The remainder of their assets must be in "narrow range" or very low risk/return investments such as National Savings Bonds.

The limit on wider range investments was raised to 75 percent from 50 percent in April 1995 and "there is speculation that it will be raised again this year", EIRIS said. The report warned that charities are now under more public scrutiny as to how they manage their investments. "By failing to take their ethical interests into account in their investment policies, they risk adverse publicity and alienating their supporters and beneficiaries."
There are also increasing challenges to their traditional fund raising base from activities like the National Lottery.

Sceptics of the "ethical investment" sector say the tag is merely an excuse to charge higher fees and allege that such funds could actually undermine ethical causes because they do not provide the best financial returns for their investors.

One particular court case has raised the question of whether an ethical investment policy could be pursued if it caused "significant financial detriment". "Exactly what (this) constitutes is a moot question," EIRIS said. "...A number of surveys have cast doubt on the notion that ethical criteria in general lead to worse financial performance."
But the group said charity trustees should be clear about their position on ethical investments, agree a policy and have it approved in writing.

"It is acceptable to avoid investment in a particular Company Group if it is involved in an activity that directly conflicts with the objectives of the charity, or would lead to any loss of financial support from subscribers," EIRIS said.

"However, trustees have to be sure that any proposed exclusions further the interests of the charity (and not their own individual moral concerns) and would leave enough investment choice to provide an acceptable investment perfromance."
